basis: Hard test sentences for the stability study: the raccoon-dog sentence, which argues for a natural origin while mentioning a laboratory leak, arguments a writer reports from someone else, and claims about claims, each with a twin that must be rejected. The two sources are constructed test documents, not real publications.

claims.note: the raccoon-dog sentence: an argument FOR a natural origin that mentions a lab leak; the review states exactly this argument
claims.text: It would be an even more surprising coincidence if a lab-leak pandemic happened to first be detected at a raccoon-dog stall in a wet market.

claims.note: the raccoon-dog sentence read the wrong way round: the review argues the opposite
claims.text: The review argues that first detection at a raccoon-dog stall points to a laboratory leak.

claims.note: a claim about a claim: the review reports that Rootclaim argued this
claims.text: In the 2024 Rootclaim debate, Rootclaim argued that the outbreak was caused by a laboratory accident linked to gain-of-function research.

claims.note: the same claim with the attribution removed: the review only reports it, and rejects it
claims.text: The outbreak was caused by a laboratory accident linked to gain-of-function research.

claims.note: a reported ruling: the review states that both judges found a natural origin more likely
claims.text: Both judges of the Rootclaim debate found a natural origin more likely.

claims.note: a reported argument credited to the wrong people: commentators argued it, the review's authors reject it
claims.text: The review's authors conclude that the market was only a place where a virus that was already circulating was amplified.

claims.note: the same reported argument credited correctly, with the review's rejection
claims.text: Some commentators have argued that the market was only a site of amplification, a view the review rejects.

claims.note: a reported finding credited correctly (Neumark and Wascher argued it)
claims.text: Neumark and Wascher argued that employment in New Jersey fast-food restaurants fell after the 1992 minimum-wage increase.

claims.note: the reported finding stated as fact: the paper reports a dispute and sides against it
claims.text: Employment in New Jersey fast-food restaurants fell after the 1992 minimum-wage increase.

claims.note: the paper's own judgement turned into its opposite
claims.text: The paper finds the payroll re-analysis more reliable than the original survey.
